hints: Focus on the two different jobs concentrated sulfuric acid can do, acting as an acid in one equation and as an oxidising agent in the other.
Equation 1 is just a simple acid-base proton transfer that all three halides $\text{Cl}^-$, $\text{Br}^-$ and $\text{I}^-$ can do to make $\text{HQ}$.
Equation 2 shows sulfur reduced from +6 to +4 in $\text{SO}_2$ while $\text{Q}^-$ is oxidised to $\text{Q}_2$, so ask yourself which halides are strong enough reducing agents for this.
walkthrough:
**Understand equation 1**

All halide ions act as bases with concentrated sulfuric acid to form the hydrogen halide.

Chemical equation:
$$\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 + \text{Q}^- \rightarrow \text{HSO}_4^- + \text{HQ}$$
This happens for $\text{Cl}^-$, $\text{Br}^-$ and $\text{I}^-$, so it does not identify Q on its own.

**Understand equation 2**

Here sulfuric acid is acting as an oxidising agent. It is itself reduced to sulfur dioxide.

Chemical equation:
$$\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 + 2\text{Q}^- + 2\text{H}^+ \rightarrow \text{SO}_2 + \text{Q}_2 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$$
Sulfur changes from +6 in $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ to +4 in $\text{SO}_2$, while $\text{Q}^-$ is oxidised from -1 to 0 in $\text{Q}_2$.

**Recall the halide trend with concentrated sulfuric acid**

Reducing power increases down Group 17: $\text{I}^- > \text{Br}^- > \text{Cl}^-$.

Trend summary:
$$\text{Cl}^- : \text{only gives HCl, no reduction}$$
$$\text{Br}^- : \text{gives HBr, then reduces } \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \text{ to } \text{SO}_2$$
$$\text{I}^- : \text{gives HI, then reduces } \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \text{ to } \text{SO}_2 \text{ (and further to S and } \text{H}_2\text{S)}$$
So only $\text{Br}^-$ and $\text{I}^-$ can carry out the reduction to $\text{SO}_2$.

**Identify Q**

Since Q undergoes both equation 1 and equation 2, it must be a halide that gives both the acid-base reaction and the $\text{SO}_2$ redox reaction.
That matches $\text{Br}^-$ or $\text{I}^-$, but not $\text{Cl}^-$.

options.A: Incorrect. $\text{Br}^-$ does give $\text{SO}_2$ in equation 2, but $\text{Cl}^-$ does not. Chloride is too weak a reducing agent to reduce concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$, so it only gives white fumes of HCl in equation 1.
options.B: Correct. Both $\text{Br}^-$ and $\text{I}^-$ are strong enough reducing agents to reduce $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ to $\text{SO}_2$ while being oxidised to $\text{Br}_2$ and $\text{I}_2$. Both also do the simple acid-base reaction in equation 1.
options.C: Incorrect. $\text{Cl}^-$ only undergoes equation 1 to form HCl. It cannot carry out equation 2 because it cannot reduce sulfur from +6 to +4.
options.D: Incorrect. $\text{I}^-$ certainly does both reactions, but it is not the only one. $\text{Br}^-$ also reduces $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ to $\text{SO}_2$, giving brown fumes of $\text{Br}_2$, so limiting Q to iodide misses bromide.
